title: experiment-traffic-chorus-and-heat-budget-notes-wip
content:
Purpose and framing:

Quick sketch of a concept: treat rollout exposure as a limited resource (heat) that multiple experiments and staged features share. The "traffic chorus" is the orchestration layer (manual + automated) that conducts which experiments sing, at what volume, and when to mute temporarily. This doc gathers cross-functional constraints, telemetry signals, allocation heuristics, and human handoffs for a light-weight heat-budget system.

Context / Why we need this:
- We run many overlapping A/B tests, canaries, and feature slices across hosted + dedicated customers.
- Uncoordinated ramps lead to noisy telemetry, false positives in regressions, and accidental SLA breaches.
- Rather than hard-throttling each experiment independently, we want a shared visibility model and a simple budget allocator that accounts for latency/cost risk and human capacity.

Core ideas (working):
- Heat budget: per-commit/timebox budget representing allowable operational 'risk' (errors, latency, cost spikes). Measured in simple units (e.g., heat points) derived from expected token-rate and past sensitivity.
- Chorus conductor: small service or operator interface that lists active experiments, their requested exposure, required signals, and current heat consumption.
- Priority lanes: safety, customer-committed, low-risk experiments. Persists into allocation decisions (safety always wins).
- Soft vs hard caps: by default we apply soft caps and progressive throttles; hard caps reserved for emergencies or regulatory contracts.

Signals we care about (must be instrumented and alerting thresholds set):
- Latency p50/p95/p99 per-model route (per-candidate).
- Error rate (5xx, model failures, parse failures) by slice.
- Quality regressions: eval-set score delta and user-facing metric deltas (CTR, accept rate) per cohort.
- Cost anomalies: tokens-per-request, per-token cost, GPU utilization cross-check.
- Downstream availability: storage/db error spikes correlated with increased load.
- Human slope: number of engineers on-call and current operational load (SRE/owner busy indicator).

Allocation heuristics (draft):
1) Request: experiment owner files exposure intent in Chorus UI (route, model variant, start, steady % goal, max heat allowance). Reference template (JIRA: PROD-4823).
2) Pre-check: automated feasibility checks (quota, model compatibility, past variant history).
3) Assign lane: system suggests lane (safety/customer/dev). Owners confirm.
4) Budget assignment: conductor suggests heat points based on model cost per token * expected qps * risk multiplier. Owners can request manual extra heat (requires approver).
5) Ramp schedule: slow-start (0.1% -> 1% -> 5% -> goal) with observations at each step. Each step consumes heat proportionally.
6) Pause/scale-back: automatic triggers reduce exposure by fraction (e.g., 50%) when threshold breaches, or human can pause.

Statistical / sampling notes (ops-friendly):
- For short microcanaries, prefer deterministic route slices (e.g., telemetry vs random) to avoid dilution.
- Minimum sample for behavioral metrics: 1k users or 5k impressions depending on metric variance — we keep a small lookup table in the Chorus UI.
- For quality-sensitive experiments (rerankers, completion scoring), require baseline eval run and pre-registered checkpoints.

Runbook excerpts (operator checklist):
- Before activation: verify linked PR, required infra (cache warming, model v pinned), and quota. Post link checklist in JIRA.
- Step ramp: kick at off-peak if possible; monitor these dashboards: model-latency, route-heat, experiment-signal. Have SRE contact ready.
- On signal breach: first action is auto-scale-back to previous stable step. If cascade continues, immediately revert exposure to 0% and notify stakeholders.
- Post-mortem: within 48 hours owner files quick incident note in JIRA and notifies #rollout-ops.

Human flows and escalation:
- Owner (product/eng) is primary contact.
- SRE is escalation point for infra issues.
- Console Oncall (telemetry owner) owns signal verification.
- Exec escapes: Product lead + Head of SRE must approve permanent re-open of heat after major incidents.

Open questions / TODOs (prioritized):
- [ ] Heat unit definition: decide on simple scalar formula or per-route lookup table (action: apply small prototype for two hosts).
- [ ] UI sketch for Chorus conductor (Jun + Marco to run mockups).
- [ ] Automated rollbacks: what fraction to reduce on first threshold breach? default 50%? (Ethan to propose).
- [ ] Integrate with Redeploy tool so model variant fallback is automatic when heat exhausted.
- [ ] Map privacy/compliance constraints: private deployments must have separate heat budgets.

Quick notes for experiments team (voice-of-owner):
- Keep pre-registered acceptance criteria simple and measurable.
- If your experiment expects heavy variability (multimodal traffic), declare it early — it will cost more heat.
- Don't try to dodge heat by sharding into many micro-slices; that breaks signal.

References / links (working):
- JIRA PROD-4823 (heat-budget prototype backlog)
- ROLL-119 (Chorus API sketch)
- Sim repo: https://github.com/redwood-inference/rollout-sim/pull/87
- Slack channel: #rollout-ops

Last thoughts: this is intentionally lightweight — aim for a low-friction conductor that provides shared accountability and prevents runaway simultaneous experiments. Next step: prototype the conductor UI and run a 2-week alpha with 3 teams (console, hosting, optimize).

Notes to self:
- run simple sim of 3 experiments competing with 100 heat pts/day and see nightly failure modes
- check if existing quota APIs can expose per-model cost estimates

- added lane heuristics 2025-12-10 (Marco)
- signal thresholds draft 2026-01-22 (Samira)
